newsitem.title: USA: Treasury vows new crackdown on tax snooping.
newsitem.headline: Treasury vows new crackdown on tax snooping.

text.p: Browsing of taxpayers' returns will not be tolerated and the Internal Revenue Service has been told to come up with a plan to stop it, a senior Treasury Department official said Tuesday.

Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers told Congress that the IRS had said in 1995 it would aggressively attempt to stop unauthorised snooping by its employees in taxpayers' records but it had failed to do so.

Testifying before a Senate subcommittee, Summers said respect for the privacy of information provided by taxpayers was "the foundation of our system of taxation." The IRS knew it and said in 1995 it would make sure that violations did not occur.

"Two years later, however, it is clear that this policy was not effectively designed or implemented and penalties are neither sufficiently consistent nor severe to put an end to unauthorised access," Summer said.
Treasury, which oversees the IRS, made its pledge to crack down on the the deadline date for individuals to file their income tax returns.
Recent reports said there were hundreds of instances in which IRS employees looked into taxpayers' records for no official reason, sometimes simply out of curiosity about celebrities' returns.

There are legislative proposals in the Senate and the House of Representatives to amend the Internal Revenue Code specifically to prohibit unauthorised access or inspection of tax returns and return information.
Summers said the proposals would "strengthen our hand in putting an end to unauthorised access" but said the IRS also needed to update its computer systems to detect and prevent such snooping.
Summers said that he and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin had ordered the IRS to report within a month "on what it proposed to do both managerially and technically to better address this problem."

Treasury has already announced a management reform plan for the IRS, which Summers said should result in sweeping changes within a year or so in how the government's tax-collecting arm is run and how it does business.
Part of that involves simplifying the 9,451-page tax code so that it easier for the IRS to administer it, Summers said.
For the foreseeable future, the United States will have an income tax that taxes people on their ability to pay, Summer said.
"Given this, it is not possible to eliminate the IRS, and it is vital that we have an IRS that functions effectively," he added.
He urged Congress to join in efforts to reform the IRS rather than to target it for partisan political battles, saying: "What we must not do is attack the IRS to promote other agendas."
